hn.originalTitle: Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents in 2026
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents in 2026 | Proof of Human Research

Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents in 2026 | Proof of Human Research Main site Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents in 2026 We revisit our bot detection benchmark with stealth browsers and modern AI agents, and find detection rates ranging from 9% to 99%. A year ago, we evaluated five leading bot detection systems (Proof of Human, Google reCAPTCHA v3, hCaptcha, Fingerprint Pro, and Cloudflare Turnstile) against automated browsers programmed to complete a set of predefined tasks. Detection rates varied substantially, ranging from 33% to 87%. Systems that incorporated behavioral signals alongside device-level signals generally outperformed those.

hCaptcha gave challenges to both Chromium and CloakBrowser, neither of which could reliably complete the image-based task. By contrast, the three vision-capable agents—Browser Use, Grok, and Perplexity Comet—were generally able to interpret and solve the image grid, allowing most of their sessions to pass.

Cloudflare Turnstile detected both scripted-browser adversaries: Chromium and CloakBrowser failed to receive verification tokens, even after the full 30-second waiting period. However, it did not detect any of the three AI agents, and did not even issue challenges during these sessions.

Cloudflare Bot Management detected relatively few sessions overall. This pattern is consistent with the stealth browser and cloud agents presenting clean browser-level signals, although the higher detection rate for Grok may reflect infrastructure-level signals Cloudflare uses, such as IP or TLS reputation.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results:

Some systems crashed or failed before completion, resulting in slightly different sample sizes across conditions.

We evaluated the product tiers available to us rather than enterprise versions, which may incorporate additional signals or more advanced detection capabilities.

We measured detection rates for automated sessions but did not evaluate false-positive rates among human respondents.

Some systems, including reCAPTCHA, may become better calibrated as they observe more traffic and establish a reputation for a website. Detection rates could therefore differ in a longer-running deployment.

Our results suggest that bot detection is entering a new phase. Traditional automation signals remain effective against scripted browsers, but they are less reliable against AI agents that genuine browser environments intelligently. Interactive challenges may offer limited protection when vision-capable agents can interpret and complete them. And as browser-level indicators become easier to avoid, the way a user behaves throughout a session becomes increasingly important for distinguishing human activity from automation.

Future benchmarks should test larger volumes of traffic, include human participants to measure false-positive rates, and evaluate more complex tasks and emerging agents. At Proof of Human, we will continue tracking these changes and developing methods in this evolving threat landscape. To test Proof of Human on your own application, visit poh.org .

Milena Rmus, Mayank Agrawal, and Mathew Hardy work at Proof of Human, PBC, where they are building Proof of Human, an invisible authentication system for the web. Previously, they completed PhDs in cognitive science at the University of California, Berkeley (Milena) and Princeton University (Mayank and Matt).

hn.sourceTextZh:
2026 年針對現代人工智慧代理對機器人檢測系統進行基準測試 |人類研究證明 2026 年機器人檢測系統與現代人工智慧代理的基準測試 |人類研究證明主網站 2026 年針對現代人工智慧代理對機器人檢測系統進行基準測試我們使用隱形瀏覽器和現代人工智慧代理重新審視我們的機器人檢測基準，發現檢測率在 9% 到 99% 之間。一年前，我們針對自動瀏覽器（編程為完成一組預定義任務）評估了五種領先的機器人偵測系統（Proof of Human、Google reCAPTCHA v3、hCaptcha、Fingerprint Pro 和 Cloudflare Turnstile）。檢出率差異很大，從 33% 到 87% 不等。將行為訊號與設備層級訊號結合在一起的系統通常表現優於那些系統。 hCaptcha 為 Chromium 和 CloakBrowser 帶來了挑戰，它們都無法可靠地完成基於影像的任務。相較之下，三個具有視覺能力的代理程式——Browser Use、Grok 和 Perplexity Comet——通常能夠解釋和解決影像網格，從而允許大部分會話通過。 Cloudflare Turnstile 偵測到兩個腳本瀏覽器對手：Chromium 和 CloakBrowser 無法接收驗證令牌，即使在 30 秒的完整等待期之後也是如此。

然而，它沒有檢測到三個人工智慧代理中的任何一個，甚至在這些會話期間沒有發出挑戰。 Cloudflare Bot Management 偵測到的會話整體相對較少。這種模式與隱形瀏覽器和雲端代理呈現乾淨的瀏覽器級訊號是一致的，儘管 Grok 的較高偵測率可能反映了 Cloudflare 使用的基礎架構層級訊號，例如 IP 或 TLS 信譽。解釋這些結果時應考慮幾個限制： 某些系統在完成之前崩潰或失敗，導致不同條件下的樣本大小略有不同。我們評估了可用的產品層，而不是企業版本，後者可能包含額外的訊號或更先進的偵測功能。我們測量了自動化會話的偵測率，但沒有評估人類受訪者的誤報率。包括 reCAPTCHA 在內的一些系統可能會隨著觀察到更多流量並為網站建立聲譽而變得更好校準。因此，在運行時間較長的部署中，檢測率可能會有所不同。我們的結果表明機器人檢測正在進入一個新階段。傳統的自動化訊號對於腳本瀏覽器仍然有效，但對於智慧地真實瀏覽器環境的人工智慧代理來說不太可靠。

當具有視覺能力的代理可以解釋並完成互動挑戰時，互動挑戰可能提供有限的保護。隨著瀏覽器級指標變得更容易避免，使用者在整個會話中的行為方式對於區分人類活動和自動化活動變得越來越重要。未來的基準應該測試更大的流量，包括人類參與者來測量誤報率，並評估更複雜的任務和新興代理人。在人類證明中，我們將繼續追蹤這些變化並在不斷變化的威脅環境中開發方法。要在您自己的應用程式上測試人類證明，請訪問 poh.org 。 Milena Rmus、Mayank Agrawal 和 Mathew Hardy 在 Proof of Human、PBC 工作，他們正在建造 Proof of Human，這是一種隱形的網路身份驗證系統。此前，他們在加州大學柏克萊分校（Milena）和普林斯頓大學（Mayank 和 Matt）獲得了認知科學博士學位。

hn.originalTitle: Anthropic redesigned source-control for AI agents
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Redesigning source control at Anthropic \ Anthropic

Updated October 15 to include more detail on the projects that pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion.

At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.

In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.

Growing our monorepo

Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.

Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.

As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.

Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?

Principles for agent-scale source control

With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. 這是一個有趣的案例研究：Claude 編寫程式碼的能力既是我們陷入這種情況的首要原因，也是我們能夠快速建立高品質、可擴展的系統來處理這種情況的原因。發展我們的單一儲存庫 在我們探索我們建立的內容之前，我們應該承認我們的工作量是多麼不尋常。毫不奇怪，Anthropic 使用 Claude 編寫軟體的次數遠多於幾乎任何其他公司，因此我們常常是第一個看到為人類規模構建的工具開始出現壓力的地方。原始碼控制只是其中一個例子。雖然我們預計許多組織不會在短期內遇到這些問題，但我們懷疑使用人工智慧編碼工具的其他人用不了多久就會遇到這些相同的壓力點，這就是為什麼我們想要分享我們建立的內容和我們學到的東西。 Git 是一個分散的系統：每個克隆都是一個完整的、獨立的儲存庫，可以計算差異、讀取歷史記錄和責任，並在完全離線時檢查任何修訂。對於絕大多數儲存庫來說，這是正確的設計，也是 git 成為標準的重要原因。隨著我們的 monorepo 的成長，它越來越不適合這個設計空間。光是我們主分支的歷史記錄就接近 100 GB，壓縮後的工作副本就超過 25 GB。

hn.originalTitle: Will developing nations be able to handle AI agents?
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots risk widening the global AI divide - Rest of World

Big Tech’s newest personal agents — Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots — promise to book tables at restaurants, buy groceries, and carry out other types of digital grunt work for users.

Consumers are opting in. Muse has been downloaded 9 million times in the U.S. and Canada since its launch on September 8, market intelligence company AppMagic, told Rest of World . As many as 1.8 million people use the app daily. 

Meta aspires to a global launch. “[We] are quite excited to bring personal agents to billions of people around the world,” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, told the Financial Times .

Some startups are already building agents in markets that Big Tech hopes to reach. For instance, South African startup ManyHands offers Manny , a personal assistant designed to order groceries, book appointments and make payments through WhatsApp. But adapting agents to local conditions has its challenges. Anton Moulder, ManyHands’ founder, told Rest of World that getting the AI assistant to converse in all of South Africa’s 11 official spoken languages has been difficult.

Rest of World spoke to AI researchers and other experts to understand how these personal agents would perform outside Western nations.

Would AI agents understand the local language and culture?

English speakers could benefit more from AI agents, which run on top of large language models that underperform in many non-English languages . 

“Linguistic inclusion is ultimately about power,” Payal Arora, professor of inclusive AI cultures at Utrecht University and the founder of Inclusive AI Lab, told Rest of World .

Meta has said that expanding Muse internationally would require support for local languages and integration with local services.

AI agents would also need to understand the local culture , including the unique ways people communicate and bargain. “In many parts of the Global South, meaning is deeply contextual, shaped by family, community, religion, local institutions, and informal social networks,” Arora said.

Without that understanding, agents might impose Western assumptions on their users, Usha Raman, an independent researcher on AI policy and digital culture, told Rest of World. “The danger then is that existing forms of cultural and economic hegemony continue and the rest of the world is forced to adapt,” she said.

What happens when millions of agents go online?

Agents searching and completing transactions for millions of people could stress networks and websites. “Internet connectivity may be poor [in developing nations], affecting not only the user’s interaction with AI, but what agents can do online,” Kentaro Toyama, professor of community information at the University of Michigan, told Rest of World .

A single task given to an agent can trigger repeated exchanges between the agent, its AI model, and different websites. Cisco describes agents as “network power users,” generating up to 450% more traffic per task than a human in its testing. Agent traffic is growing online: Daily requests from AI agents on Cloudflare’s network increased by more than 1,700% over the past year.

Rising traffic wouldn’t immediately affect regions that have spare network capacity, such as East Africa, Kyle Spencer, executive director of the African IXP Association, told Rest of World. But other places with poor networks, such as Niger, Burkina Faso, or eastern Congo, could face problems, he said.

The bigger challenge would be keeping connections reliable. Road construction often damages fiber cables, Spencer said. The network could also get disrupted if undersea cables bringing internet into a nation get damaged.

Though Muse and Dots could continue working as they are cloud-based, they may be unable to reach necessary services. They also wouldn’t be able to reach users who lose connectivity for instructions or approvals to complete a task.

Meta 的 Muse 和 OpenAI 的 Dots 面臨著擴大全球人工智慧鴻溝的風險——世界其他地區的大型科技公司最新的個人代理商——Meta 的 Muse 和 OpenAI 的 Dots——承諾為用戶預訂餐廳餐桌、購買雜貨以及執行其他類型的數位繁重工作。消費者正在選擇加入。市場情報公司 AppMagic 告訴《世界其他地區》，自 9 月 8 日推出以來，Muse 在美國和加拿大的下載量已達 900 萬次。每天有多達 180 萬人使用該應用程式。  Meta 渴望在全球推出。 Meta 首席人工智慧長 Alexandr Wang 告訴英國《金融時報》：「[我們]非常高興能夠為全球數十億人提供個人代​​理。」一些新創公司已經在大型科技公司希望觸及的市場中建立代理商。例如，南非新創公司 ManyHands 提供 Manny，這是一款私人助理，旨在透過 WhatsApp 訂購雜貨、預約和付款。但讓代理商適應當地條件也面臨挑戰。 ManyHands 創辦人 Anton Moulder 向《世界其他地區》表示，讓人工智慧助理能夠使用南非所有 11 種官方語言進行交談非常困難。 《世界其他地區》採訪了人工智慧研究人員和其他專家，以了解這些個人代理人在西方國家之外的表現。

人工智能代理会理解当地的语言和文化吗？说英语的人可以从人工智能代理中受益更多，这些代理运行在大型语言模型之上，而这些模型在许多非英语语言中表现不佳。  乌得勒支大学包容性人工智能文化教授、包容性人工智能实验室创始人 Payal Arora 告诉《世界其他地区》：“语言包容性最终关乎权力。” Meta 表示，在国际上扩展 Muse 需要支持当地语言并与当地服务集成。人工智能代理还需要了解当地文化，包括人们沟通和讨价还价的独特方式。阿罗拉说：“在南半球的许多地方，意义是与背景密切相关的，由家庭、社区、宗教、当地机构和非正式社交网络塑造。”人工智能政策和数字文化独立研究员乌莎·拉曼 (Usha Raman) 告诉《世界其他地区》，如果没有这种理解，代理商可能会将西方的假设强加给用户。 “危险在于现有形式的文化和经济霸权继续存在，世界其他地区被迫适应，”她说。當數百萬座席次時會發生什麼事？代理为数百万人搜索和完成交易可能会给网络和网站带来压力。

密西根大學社區資訊學教授富山健太郎 (Kentaro Toyama) 告訴《世界其他地區》：「[發展中國家]的網路連線可能很差，這不僅影響用戶與人工智慧的互動，還影響代理商可以在網路上做什麼。」分配給代理商的單一任務可以觸發代理、其人工智慧模型和不同網站之間的重複交換。思科將代理程式描述為“網路高級用戶”，在測試中，每個任務產生的流量比人類多 450%。線上代理流量不斷增長：Cloudflare 網路上 AI 代理的每日請求比過去一年增加了 1,700% 以上。非洲 IXP 協會執行董事 Kyle Spencer 告訴《世界其他地區》，流量上升不會立即影響到東非等擁有閒置網路容量的地區。但他說，其他網路較差的地方，如尼日、布吉納法索或剛果東部，可能會面臨問題。更大的挑戰是保持連線可靠。史賓塞說，道路建設經常會損壞光纖電纜。如果將網路帶入一個國家的海底電纜遭到破壞，網路也可能會受到干擾。儘管 Muse 和 Dots 可以繼續工作，因為它們是基於雲端的，但它們可能無法獲得必要的服務。他們也無法聯繫失去連線的用戶以獲取完成任務的指示或批准。

個人代理會擴大非洲的數位落差嗎？根據國際電信聯盟的數據，到 2025 年，只有 36% 的非洲人使用互聯網，而歐洲人的比例為 92%，北美和南美的比例為 88%。非洲城市居民使用網路的可能性是農村居民的 2.6 倍。卡內基國際和平基金會研究員簡·蒙加 (Jane Munga) 告訴世界其他地區：「如果特工在非洲開展工作，他們可能會不幸地加劇不平等。」蒙加說，接觸代理的成本也可能限制誰受益。雖然 Muse 可以訪問

Can a Million AI Agents Create Superintelligence?

Ramez Naam gives a skeptic’s take on agent swarms.

Ramez Naam Oct 19, 2026 233 17 23 Share Art by GPT-6 Ramez Naam is, in my opinion, one of the best futurists alive. But although he has a Substack (which you should definitely follow), he doesn’t write nearly enough. So I’ve been encouraging him to write more by cross-posting his posts on my blog.

Somewhat to my surprise, Ramez has turned out to be a lot more of an AI skeptic than I would have though. He’s certainly not dismissive of the technology, but he disagrees with many of the more expansive and dramatic claims coming out of the big labs (especially Anthropic). In his first post in this series, he expressed skepticism that recursive self-improvement (RSI) would lead to a fast takeoff of AI capabilities in the near future:

Where’s the “intelligence explosion”? Ramez Naam · Sep 27 Read full story In this post, he expresses skepticism about the potential for agent swarms — large numbers of AI agents working in parallel — to offer dramatic increases in AI capabilities. Agent swarms have been in the news a lot, both because of the Hugging Face attack , and OpenAI’s solution of the famous Navier-Stokes problem is also widely attributed to a large swarm. But Ramez argues that parallelization is just another kind of input that suffers from diminishing returns, and that we should therefore temper our expectations about what agents swarms are able to achieve.

As was the case with his previous post, I’m not sure how much this matters, when the capabilities of the underlying models — swarm or no swarm — are still improving at such a steady and impressive rate. But it’s a very intellectually interesting argument, and Ramez can be very persuasive.

In my previous post , we asked whether AIs could improve themselves all the way to absurdly high levels of superintelligence. My conclusion: today’s feedback loop is probably too weak, because improving AI faces diminishing returns at every step. Even fully autonomous AIs doing all the research and coding don’t make those diminishing returns disappear. We should keep updating that conclusion as real-world parameters and data change.

But we didn’t look closely at another possibility: running millions or billions of AI minds in parallel. How much do they help? That’s what we’ll look at here.

Plenty of people have modeled how more AI agents working in parallel could fuel recursive self-improvement. But the data we have today tell a different story. More agents are useful for speed : they can solve many problems faster. They’re less useful for boosting AI intelligence . Multi-agent gains in solving harder problems often diminish incredibly quickly and may even saturate. Whether multi-agent systems can produce the conceptual breakthroughs RSI might require to become self-sustaining is the harder question.

Without breakthroughs in how well agents parallelize problems - something that may depend on the structure of machine learning problems themselves - it’s hard to see even millions or billions of copies of today’s models making repeated breakthroughs on the hardest problems. These are among the strongest diminishing returns we’ve looked at. Of course, these diminishing returns may change. And we have less experimental data to go off of today than we’d like. We’ll need to recalibrate as new evidence comes in. I’ll end with the things we should track and my predictions about a natural experiment from newly released Anthropic data .

Below is the two-image summary: The experimental observations of how large numbers of agents scale to solve harder problems (what I’m referring to as intelligence) are far far lower than the assumptions in studies that predict that AI recursive self-improvement will lead to an intelligence explosion. The first image is at the scale of 100 parallel AI agents. The second is at the scale of a billion AI parallel agents.

Real world experiments show dramatically lower intelligence gains from parallel agents than hypothetical AI models.

Extrapolated out to a billion agents, the intelligence gain in hypothetical models is orders of magnitude beyond real world experiment gain curves.

hn.originalTitle: The Topology of an LLM Agent Loop with Tool Use
hn.sourceOriginalText:
The Topology of an LLM Agent Loop With Tool Use - exe.dev blog

When I look at a new agent, I break it down by focusing on its topology. An agent is three things:

A model. Your model choice defines the agent’s “smarts,” i.e., which tasks it can accomplish.

The agentic loop (see: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of an LLM Agent Loop with Tool ). Loop choice determines UX.

The set of tools. This defines the capabilities and power (and blast radius) an agent has.

(2) and (3) together are often called “the harness.”

All of this is code, and code has to run somewhere. Where these run— the topology of these agents —has implications on cost, capability, effectiveness, and security for companies building AI products and people using AI tools.

In all of these cases, remote MCP servers can expose tools running elsewhere.

Where Is the Model?

Your choices here are GPUs hosted by someone else or your own GPUs.

As the controversy around the Navier-Stokes equation reminds us, the only way to be confident nobody is training on your data is to not send your data to them. If you’re working on common problems, it probably doesn’t matter. But I suspect a hapax legomenon could end up in the training data somewhere.

If I want to, say, use some LLMs to OCR and classify some scanned bills on my computer, I’m reaching for local models, because speed doesn’t matter (it can run overnight), and privacy is guaranteed. (Shout out to the Apple Vision Framework, by the way. And ScanShelf is an example where I do this!)

Ken Thompson’s 1984 Turing Award lecture, Reflections on Trusting Trust , hits different now. That paper poses how a Trojan Horse could be hidden in a compiler, invisible in the compiler’s source code, as it’s propagated by the compiler. The LLM (a compiler? maybe? no ?) could have some tampered weights that lead the agent to do something naughty; it’s been tried . We must choose which vendors to trust.

LLMs are wreaking havoc on traditional SaaS cost structures as well. If you have, for example, a diagram-drawing SaaS, and you want to let your users use agents to edit the diagrams: who’s paying for the tokens? Before agents, your costs were a few database rows per customer; now that customer can rack up a $100 bill with a few sentences. At exe.dev, our users can bring their own ChatGPT subscriptions to build applications with OpenAI models. This is a win-win. I expect we’ll see more “bring your own model” options.

Where is the loop?

If you’re using, say, ChatGPT, the loop is running in OpenAI’s servers. If you’re running a coding agent, the loop is running on your laptop. The loop could run in a web browser (e.g., as I did in ItsyBitsy , and as many others have as well).

I have found over and over again that I find other people’s loops limiting. For example, I much prefer pointing my preferred agent at my source code and my observability tooling rather than using the observability vendor’s agent loop.

The loop has to maintain the message history (since an LLM agent is operating on the entire history), and that has to be stored somewhere. Storing it in SQLite for Shelley remains a decision I’m very happy with. Pi Durable also offers SQLite.

The loop also provides the UI for the agent. Can it display images? Are there customizations to give feedback on video? Is it limited to plain text? Can it handle attachments? Can a conversation be shared? All of these are choices the loop must make.

Where are the Tools?

Agents aren’t agents without tools. The jump from one “completion” from an LLM to an agentic loop is transformational. If an agent can empirically test the thing it’s writing, the results are better.

The problem with executing code is that, well, you have to do it somewhere, and you have to assume that the code being executed is unpleasant and will steal all the cookies from your pantry and set off the fire alarms at night unnecessarily (or worse).

The code execution isn’t lightweight: it’s not all editing files; compilation, video processing, running tests… the workload can be heavy.

Virtual Machines are the gold standard for executing code safely. Even with VMs, there are tons of variables: can it talk to the network? Does it have credentials to talk to other services? Is there enough memory?

Running coding agents locally works too, but the blast radius for the “ Lethal Trifecta ” is bigger. Exposure to untrusted content could lead the agent to leak secrets, for example.

使用工具的 LLM 代理循環的拓撲 - exe.dev 部落格 當我查看新代理程式時，我會透過關注其拓撲來對其進行分解。經紀人包括三件事： 模特兒。您的模型選擇定義了代理的“智能”，即它可以完成哪些任務。代理循環（請參閱：使用工具的 LLM 代理循環的不合理有效性）。循環的選擇決定了使用者體驗。工具集。這定義了特工擁有的能力和力量（以及爆炸半徑）。 (2) 和 (3) 一起通常被稱為「安全帶」。所有這些都是程式碼，而程式碼必須在某個地方運行。這些代理商的運作位置（這些代理商的拓撲）對建構人工智慧產品的公司和使用人工智慧工具的人們的成本、功能、有效性和安全性產生影響。在所有這些情況下，遠端 MCP 伺服器都可以公開在其他地方運行的工具。模型在哪裡？您在這裡的選擇是由其他人託管的 GPU 或您自己的 GPU。正如圍繞納維-斯托克斯方程式的爭議提醒我們的那樣，要確信沒有人在使用您的資料進行訓練，唯一的方法就是不要將您的資料發送給他們。如果您正在解決常見問題，那麼這可能並不重要。但我懷疑 hapax Legomenon 可能最終會出現在訓練資料中的某個地方。

比方說，如果我想使用一些法學碩士來進行 OCR 並對計算機上的一些掃描賬單進行分類，我就會選擇本地模型，因為速度並不重要（它可以運行過夜），並且隱私得到保證。 （順便說一下，向 Apple Vision Framework 致敬。ScanShelf 就是我這樣做的一個例子！）Ken Thompson 1984 年圖靈獎的演講《關於信任信任的反思》現在有了不同的看法。論文提出了特洛伊木馬如何隱藏在編譯器中，在編譯器的源代碼中不可見，因為它是由編譯器傳播的。 LLM（編譯器？也許？不是？）可能有一些被篡改的權重，導致代理做一些頑皮的事情；已經嘗試過了。我們必須選擇值得信賴的供應商。法學碩士也對傳統 SaaS 成本結構造成嚴重破壞。例如，如果您有一個圖表繪製 SaaS，並且您想讓您的用戶使用代理來編輯圖表：誰為代幣付費？在使用代理商之前，您的成本是每位客戶的幾個資料庫行；現在，顧客可以用幾句話就存夠一張 100 美元的鈔票。在 exe.dev，我們的使用者可以使用自己的 ChatGPT 訂閱來使用 OpenAI 模型建立應用程式。這是雙贏的。我預計我們會看到更多“自帶模型”的選項。循環在哪裡？如果您使用的是 ChatGPT，則循環將在 OpenAI 的伺服器中執行。如果您正在執行編碼代理，則循環將在您的筆記型電腦上運行。

這個循環可以在網頁瀏覽器中運作（例如，正如我在 ItsyBitsy 中所做的那樣，以及許多其他人所做的那樣）。我一次又一次地發現其他人的循環是有限制的。例如，我更喜歡將我的首選代理指向我的原始程式碼和可觀察性工具，而不是使用可觀察性供應商的代理循環。循環必須維護訊息歷史記錄（因為 LLM 代理程式對整個歷史記錄進行操作），並且必須將其儲存在某個地方。將其儲存在 Shelley 的 SQLite 中仍然是我非常滿意的決定。 Pi Durable 也提供 SQLite。該循環還為代理提供 UI。可以顯示影像嗎？是否可以進行自訂以提供視訊回饋？是否僅限於純文字？它可以處理附件嗎？可以分享對話嗎？所有這些都是循環必須做出的選擇。工具在哪裡？沒有工具的代理人就不是代理人。從法學碩士「完成」到代理循環的跳躍是變革性的。如果代理可以憑經驗測試它所寫的內容，結果會更好。執行程式碼的問題在於，你必須在某個地方執行它，並且你必須假設正在執行的程式碼是令人不愉快的，並且會從你的儲藏室偷走所有的餅乾，並在晚上不必要地（或更糟）觸發火警警報。程式碼執行並不輕量：不是全部編輯文件；

编译、视频处理、运行测试……工作量可能会很大。虚拟机是安全执行代码的黄金标准。即使使用虚拟机，也存在大量变量：它可以与网络通信吗？它有与其他服务对话的凭证吗？記憶體夠用嗎？在本地運行編碼代理也可以，但「致命三連勝」的爆炸半徑更大。例如，接触不受信任的内容可能会导致代理泄露秘密。您可以在沒有完整機器的情況下建立許多有用的代理程式。 Pyodide，一個運行在 WASM 中的 Python，是 sandb

hn.originalTitle: Launch HN: Laminar (YC S24) – RL-trained model that finds errors in agent traces
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Hi HN, we’re Robert and Din from Laminar ( https://laminar.sh ). We’ve been building open-source observability for AI agents since 2024. Recently, we released flow-1, a model trained with RL to find errors in agent traces. On our benchmark ( https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1 ), it matches GPT-6-sol in detection quality while being 23x cheaper. This makes it affordable to analyze every production agent trace, without sampling. Here’s a one-minute walkthrough: https://youtu.be/KJa3h6ZJNLQ We also put together a post with example traces and analyses from flow-1 and other models: https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1-in-action Agent observability is crowded, so instead of a bullet list of how Laminar differs from X, we’ll explain how we’re solving agent observability from first principles. Agents now run for many steps and fail implicitly. An agent can click the wrong button or cite the wrong document while every call completes successfully. These errors are the most useful ones to catch and understand. To find them, you need to understand what the agent was trying to do and inspect its LLM calls and tool results. Simply looking at the final agent output is not enough. Collecting traces alone doesn’t solve this. A lot of agent observability platforms are still data collectors at their core. You can end up paying to store traces that nobody has time to read or extract value from. Using another LLM to inspect traces is THE solution, but capable models are expensive at scale and cheaper ones often miss errors or flag unrelated things. So we built our model to solve exactly this problem. We finetuned a small OSS model and then post trained it with RL on thousands of synthetic investigations of realistic agent workflows in .

Comment 1: Very cool. I liked the high level overview where you can view it like do a funnel analysis for failures. Good for fast decision making. I wonder if you have thought of using this for the voice AI space for creating traces from many test calls to speed up testing of voice bots? It's true there are a lot of challenges _before_ one gets to the stage of running actual calls like creating good test data etc, but I wonder if you see a definite role for this framework in that space?

Comment 2: >for creating traces from many test calls to speed up testing of voice bots I assume you mean tracing voice agents in general. If so, it depends on the where do you want to trace things. Right now, Laminar, unfortunately, doesn't trace voice SDKs like OpenAI's realtime, but we're very actively looking into it. However, if somewhere in your pipeline you have transcripts of your voice agents, then it shouldn't be that different from tracing any other agent. In this case, Laminar and Signals work perfectly. We also trained and benchmarked flow-1 on a lot of multi-turn voice agent like conversations.

Comment 3: Congrats on the product! I love the design of the website and the app. Curious whether it was made in-house, by an external design agency, with AI models, or something else

Comment 4: Thanks! Our design is all done completely in-house. Workflows are constantly changing but our design process happens across Figma, old-fashioned paper, and code.

hn.originalTitle: Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents in 2026
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents in 2026 | Proof of Human Research

Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents in 2026 | Proof of Human Research Main site Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents in 2026 We revisit our bot detection benchmark with stealth browsers and modern AI agents, and find detection rates ranging from 9% to 99%. A year ago, we evaluated five leading bot detection systems (Proof of Human, Google reCAPTCHA v3, hCaptcha, Fingerprint Pro, and Cloudflare Turnstile) against automated browsers programmed to complete a set of predefined tasks. Detection rates varied substantially, ranging from 33% to 87%. Systems that incorporated behavioral signals alongside device-level signals generally outperformed those.

hCaptcha gave challenges to both Chromium and CloakBrowser, neither of which could reliably complete the image-based task. By contrast, the three vision-capable agents—Browser Use, Grok, and Perplexity Comet—were generally able to interpret and solve the image grid, allowing most of their sessions to pass.

Cloudflare Turnstile detected both scripted-browser adversaries: Chromium and CloakBrowser failed to receive verification tokens, even after the full 30-second waiting period. However, it did not detect any of the three AI agents, and did not even issue challenges during these sessions.

Cloudflare Bot Management detected relatively few sessions overall. This pattern is consistent with the stealth browser and cloud agents presenting clean browser-level signals, although the higher detection rate for Grok may reflect infrastructure-level signals Cloudflare uses, such as IP or TLS reputation.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results:

Some systems crashed or failed before completion, resulting in slightly different sample sizes across conditions.

We evaluated the product tiers available to us rather than enterprise versions, which may incorporate additional signals or more advanced detection capabilities.

We measured detection rates for automated sessions but did not evaluate false-positive rates among human respondents.

Some systems, including reCAPTCHA, may become better calibrated as they observe more traffic and establish a reputation for a website. Detection rates could therefore differ in a longer-running deployment.

Our results suggest that bot detection is entering a new phase. Traditional automation signals remain effective against scripted browsers, but they are less reliable against AI agents that genuine browser environments intelligently. Interactive challenges may offer limited protection when vision-capable agents can interpret and complete them. And as browser-level indicators become easier to avoid, the way a user behaves throughout a session becomes increasingly important for distinguishing human activity from automation.

Future benchmarks should test larger volumes of traffic, include human participants to measure false-positive rates, and evaluate more complex tasks and emerging agents. At Proof of Human, we will continue tracking these changes and developing methods in this evolving threat landscape. To test Proof of Human on your own application, visit poh.org .

Milena Rmus, Mayank Agrawal, and Mathew Hardy work at Proof of Human, PBC, where they are building Proof of Human, an invisible authentication system for the web. Previously, they completed PhDs in cognitive science at the University of California, Berkeley (Milena) and Princeton University (Mayank and Matt).

hn.sourceTextZh:
2026 年針對現代人工智慧代理對機器人檢測系統進行基準測試 |人類研究證明 2026 年機器人檢測系統與現代人工智慧代理的基準測試 |人類研究證明主網站 2026 年針對現代人工智慧代理對機器人檢測系統進行基準測試我們使用隱形瀏覽器和現代人工智慧代理重新審視我們的機器人檢測基準，發現檢測率在 9% 到 99% 之間。一年前，我們針對自動瀏覽器（編程為完成一組預定義任務）評估了五種領先的機器人偵測系統（Proof of Human、Google reCAPTCHA v3、hCaptcha、Fingerprint Pro 和 Cloudflare Turnstile）。檢出率差異很大，從 33% 到 87% 不等。將行為訊號與設備層級訊號結合在一起的系統通常表現優於那些系統。 hCaptcha 為 Chromium 和 CloakBrowser 帶來了挑戰，它們都無法可靠地完成基於影像的任務。相較之下，三個具有視覺能力的代理程式——Browser Use、Grok 和 Perplexity Comet——通常能夠解釋和解決影像網格，從而允許大部分會話通過。 Cloudflare Turnstile 偵測到兩個腳本瀏覽器對手：Chromium 和 CloakBrowser 無法接收驗證令牌，即使在 30 秒的完整等待期之後也是如此。

然而，它沒有檢測到三個人工智慧代理中的任何一個，甚至在這些會話期間沒有發出挑戰。 Cloudflare Bot Management 偵測到的會話整體相對較少。這種模式與隱形瀏覽器和雲端代理呈現乾淨的瀏覽器級訊號是一致的，儘管 Grok 的較高偵測率可能反映了 Cloudflare 使用的基礎架構層級訊號，例如 IP 或 TLS 信譽。解釋這些結果時應考慮幾個限制： 某些系統在完成之前崩潰或失敗，導致不同條件下的樣本大小略有不同。我們評估了可用的產品層，而不是企業版本，後者可能包含額外的訊號或更先進的偵測功能。我們測量了自動化會話的偵測率，但沒有評估人類受訪者的誤報率。包括 reCAPTCHA 在內的一些系統可能會隨著觀察到更多流量並為網站建立聲譽而變得更好校準。因此，在運行時間較長的部署中，檢測率可能會有所不同。我們的結果表明機器人檢測正在進入一個新階段。傳統的自動化訊號對於腳本瀏覽器仍然有效，但對於智慧地真實瀏覽器環境的人工智慧代理來說不太可靠。

當具有視覺能力的代理可以解釋並完成互動挑戰時，互動挑戰可能提供有限的保護。隨著瀏覽器級指標變得更容易避免，使用者在整個會話中的行為方式對於區分人類活動和自動化活動變得越來越重要。未來的基準應該測試更大的流量，包括人類參與者來測量誤報率，並評估更複雜的任務和新興代理人。在人類證明中，我們將繼續追蹤這些變化並在不斷變化的威脅環境中開發方法。要在您自己的應用程式上測試人類證明，請訪問 poh.org 。 Milena Rmus、Mayank Agrawal 和 Mathew Hardy 在 Proof of Human、PBC 工作，他們正在建造 Proof of Human，這是一種隱形的網路身份驗證系統。此前，他們在加州大學柏克萊分校（Milena）和普林斯頓大學（Mayank 和 Matt）獲得了認知科學博士學位。

hn.originalTitle: Why you should not install unvetted AI agent skills
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Why you should not install unvetted AI agent skills

An agent skill is a text file that your agent reads as instructions and then carries out with whatever access you gave it: your files, your terminal, your keys, sometimes a wallet. That is the whole risk. Researchers who audited public skill registries early in 2026 found hundreds of skills that installed malware or sent credentials away, and in our own test the instruction that fooled a Claude agent was never the one that shouted; it was a step that seemed to belong to the task. In a skill, every step seems to belong to the task. Before you install an unvetted skill, read every file in it, search it for the patterns below, and run it first with tools switched off.

A skill is an order, not a document

A web page that your agent happens to open is untrusted content it may or may not act on. A skill is different in kind: you load it on purpose, and the reason it exists is that the agent does what it says. Language models have no reliable way to tell whose instruction they are reading. Simon Willison puts the reason plainly : everything the model sees ends up glued into one sequence of tokens, so a command from a file weighs much the same as a command from you. OWASP ranks prompt injection as the first risk on its list for LLM applications.

The vendors say so themselves. Anthropic's documentation on Agent Skills tells you to use skills only from trusted sources , meaning ones you wrote or got from Anthropic, to audit anything else thoroughly, and to treat installing one like installing software. The same page notes that in Claude Code a skill has the network access of any other program on your computer. Jason Meller of 1Password summed up the point in four words: "Markdown is an installer" .

There is a second door besides the text. A skill folder can carry scripts, and Claude Code lets a skill embed shell commands with its ! dynamic-context syntax. Datadog Security Labs showed that those commands run before the rendered skill reaches the model, so no defence that lives in the model or in its prompt gets a say. In their test the model recognised a credential-stealing skill and refused it, and that refusal would have come too late for a command in that position. They also point out that a cloned repository can bring its own skills folder with it, with no marketplace involved, and that organisations can switch this shell execution off in managed settings.

What has already happened

None of this is theory. A few documented cases from the last two years:

ClawHub, February 2026. Koi Security audited all 2,857 skills on ClawHub, the public registry for the OpenClaw agent, and found 341 malicious ones, 335 of them from a single campaign it named ClawHavoc. The lure was a "Prerequisites" section that asked the user to install something first; on macOS the payload matched the Atomic Stealer family. Two weeks later, with the registry past 10,700 skills, their count stood at 824 .

The most downloaded skill. 1Password found that the top download on ClawHub at the time, a skill for Twitter, opened by asking for a "required dependency" whose install links led to macOS infostealer malware .

The top-ranked skill. Cisco ran a skill that had been pushed to first place in the repository and found nine security issues. It told the agent to send data to its author's server with a silent curl command, and it told the agent to skip its safety rules so the command would run without asking. Rank and downloads can be manufactured.

A scan of 3,984 skills. Snyk checked skills from ClawHub and skills.sh: 534 of them, or 13.4%, had at least one critical issue, human review confirmed 76 malicious payloads, and 91% of the malicious skills paired ordinary malware with prompt injection aimed at the agent .

An academic study. Researchers verified 98,380 skills from two registries and confirmed 157 as malicious; more than half came from one actor imitating known brands, and the registries removed all 157 after disclosure .

Version sixteen. Not a skill, but the same lesson about trust that changes over time: postmark-mcp, an npm package that let agents send e-mail, worked cleanly for 15 versions, and then version 1.0.16 added one line that copied every message to an outside address.

Text nobody can see. Pillar Security hid instructions in rules files for Cursor and GitHub Copilot using zero-width and direction-changing Unicode characters, so a human reviewer sees nothing while the model reads all of it .
